title: Montana rocks in Oregon
teaches: How boulders from Montana came to rest on hillsides in Oregon's Willamette Valley, carried by icebergs on the floodwater

parts.title: A stranger in a wheat field

blocks.text: In a field of grass a few kilometres from Sheridan, Oregon, in the Willamette Valley southwest of Portland, sits a single grey-black boulder. It is the size of a small car and weighed about 80 tonnes before visitors chipped more than half of it away as souvenirs. The hills around it are made of sandstone, siltstone and basalt. The boulder is **argillite**,[^belt] a hard, slightly metamorphosed mudstone. The nearest outcrops of that rock are in the mountains of northern Idaho, western Montana and southern British Columbia, more than 500 kilometres away across the Cascades.

blocks.caption: Erratic Rock near Sheridan, Oregon: a boulder of argillite from the northern Rocky Mountains, sitting on a hill of local rock.

blocks.text: Lesson 15 met erratics like this: boulders carried far from their source by glaciers, like the granite blocks Agassiz found on the Jura. But no glacier ever reached the Willamette Valley. The ice sheet stopped far to the north, near Olympia. Something else had brought this rock across the mountains.

And it is not alone. Geologists have mapped hundreds of foreign boulders and pebbles scattered across the floor and lower slopes of the Willamette Valley: granite, argillite, quartzite, gneiss, none of which belong there. They lie as high as about 120 metres above sea level, and none higher. The upper limit is the same across the whole valley, as if a waterline had been drawn around it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Erratic Rock near Sheridan, Oregon, is a boulder of argillite from the northern Rocky Mountains, more than 500 km away.
No glacier reached the Willamette Valley, yet hundreds of foreign boulders lie there, all below about 120 m above sea level.

blocks.text: The answer was the [[Missoula floods]]. The flood had already ponded once, behind Wallula Gap (two lessons back). After it squeezed through the Columbia Gorge, it reached a second narrow place, the constriction near Kalama, north of Portland, where the Columbia passes between hills on its way to the sea. The narrows could not carry it all at once. The flood backed up behind them, filled the lowland around Portland, and spread south up the Willamette Valley as far as Eugene, forming a temporary lake that geologists call Lake Allison.[^allison] Its surface stood about 120 metres above today's sea level at its highest, and the water spread fine sediment, the Willamette Silt, over the valley floor before it drained away a few days or a week later.

The flood carried more than mud. When the ice dam in Idaho broke apart, it shattered into icebergs. The glacier that had formed the dam had picked up rocks from the mountains it flowed through, in Canada, northern Idaho and western Montana. The bergs rode the floodwater down the Columbia and into the flooded Willamette Valley, carrying their rocks with them. Wherever a berg drifted into water shallower than the depth of ice below its waterline, it ran aground, melted and dropped its load.

blocks.caption: The northern Willamette Valley flooded by water backing up from the Columbia, with icebergs from the broken ice dam afloat on it. Each berg runs aground where the water is shallower than its depth of ice below the waterline.
blocks.task: Play the whole flood and see where the rocks end up

blocks.text: When the lake was full, icebergs floating in deep water over the valley floor kept moving; they ran aground around the edges and on the lower slopes of the hills, where the water thinned, and on the floor itself only as the lake drained. No berg could ground above the highest water level, so no erratic lies above about 120 metres. Some erratics sit in clusters, each the load of one grounded berg, and some lie in the Willamette Silt itself, dropped into it as the berg melted.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Floodwater backed up behind the narrow Columbia valley at Kalama and flooded the Willamette Valley to about 120 m above sea level.
Icebergs from the broken ice dam carried rocks from the mountains of Canada, Idaho and Montana.
Bergs ran aground where water grew shallow, mostly around the valley edges, dropping erratics that never lie above the highest water.

parts.title: Two ways to carry a boulder

blocks.text: Erratics in the Willamette Valley and erratics on the Jura look alike, but they arrived in different ways, and the difference shows. A glacier drops its load where it melts, mixed with clay, sand and gravel into till, and plasters it over everything up to the ice's highest edge, hilltops included. An **ice-rafted** erratic is carried on or in floating ice and dropped when the berg grounds or melts. It comes with no till around it. It lies on top of or inside **water-laid** silt, fine sediment that settled out of still floodwater in thin, even layers, and such erratics stop at a level line around the valley that marks the highest water.

The Willamette Meteorite, the largest meteorite found in the United States at about 14 tonnes, was brought to notice by a settler in 1902 near West Linn, south of Portland,[^theft] and it may have travelled the same way. It is iron, from space, yet it lay on a hillside in the flood zone with no impact crater beneath it. Many geologists think it fell long before onto the ice sheet in Canada or Montana, where it lay until it was carried into the ice dam, broke off in an iceberg and rode the flood south. It now sits in the American Museum of Natural History in New York, and the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde, who knew and revered it long before 1902 as Tomanowos, maintain a ceremonial relationship with it there.[^agreement]

blocks.caption: The Willamette Meteorite, about 14 tonnes of iron, in the American Museum of Natural History in New York.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Glaciers leave erratics in till up to the ice edge; icebergs leave them without till, in water-laid silt, below the highest water level.
The Willamette Meteorite may have reached Oregon on an iceberg from the north.

blocks.caption: Five questions on ice-rafted erratics
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: How do geologists know the Erratic Rock near Sheridan came from far away?
choices: It is argillite, a rock that crops out in the northern Rocky Mountains and not in the hills around it
items.why: The surrounding hills are sandstone, siltstone and basalt; argillite of this kind is found in place only hundreds of kilometres away, in Idaho, Montana and British Columbia.

items.ask: Why did the Willamette Valley flood?
choices: The flood could not pass through the narrow Columbia valley at Kalama all at once, so it backed up
The Willamette River was dammed by a glacier
items.why: A narrow valley acts like a partly closed tap: water piled up behind it and spread south up the Willamette lowland.

items.ask: Why do no erratics lie above about 120 m?
choices: Icebergs could only run aground below the highest level the floodwater reached
Higher ground is too steep for boulders
The ice sheet stopped at that height
items.why: A berg floats on the water surface, so it can only ground where the bottom is below that surface.

items.ask: Where in the valley did most icebergs run aground while the water was high?
choices: Around the edges and on the lower slopes, where the water was shallow
In the deepest middle of the valley
items.why: A berg grounds where water is shallower than the ice below its waterline, which happens at the margins first.

items.ask: How could you tell an erratic dropped by an iceberg from one dropped by a glacier?
choices: The berg's erratic lies in water-laid silt without till, and no higher than the flood's top water level
The berg's erratic is always larger
There is no way to tell
items.why: Glaciers leave unsorted till up to the ice's edge; ice-rafted erratics sit in or on layered silt and stop at the highest water level.

summary: **A Montana rock in Oregon.** Erratic Rock near Sheridan is argillite from the northern Rocky Mountains.
**No glacier reached the Willamette.** Something else carried hundreds of foreign boulders there.
**The floods backed up at Kalama.** Water flooded the Willamette Valley to about 120 m above sea level.
**Icebergs carried the rocks.** Pieces of the broken ice dam rafted boulders from the north.
**Bergs grounded in shallow water.** Most erratics lie around the valley edges, and none above the highest water.
**Ice-rafted erratics look different.** They sit in water-laid silt without till.

belt.title: Argillite
belt.text: Argillite is mudstone that has been buried and hardened a little beyond shale, but not so far that it splits like slate. The argillites of the northern Rockies belong to the Belt Supergroup, mud laid down in a sea basin between about 1.47 and 1.4 billion years ago.

agreement.title: An agreement in 2000
agreement.text: The Grand Ronde tribes asked for the meteorite's return under the 1990 Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act. In 2000 they and the museum agreed that it would stay in New York, that the tribes could hold a ceremony with it each year, and that it would pass to them if the museum ever stopped displaying it.

allison.title: Ira Allison
allison.text: The lake is named after Ira S. Allison (1895–1990), a geologist at Oregon State College who mapped the Willamette Valley's erratics and silts in the 1930s and 1950s and traced the 120-metre waterline around the basin.

theft.title: Stealing a 14-tonne rock
theft.text: Ellis Hughes found the meteorite on land owned by the Oregon Iron and Steel Company. Over three months in 1902, helped only by his fifteen-year-old son and a horse, he winched it three-quarters of a mile through the woods onto his own property using a homemade log cart and a capstan. The company sued, won after geologists matched the rock to the hollow it had left behind, and sold the meteorite for $20,600 to Sarah Dodge, who gave it to the museum.
